historical_timeline.summary: Training for long-distance running around Wilmslow.
Tried for gross indecency; accepts a year of oestrogen treatment instead of prison; loses his security clearance.
Decides to see a psychiatrist again and begins Jungian analysis.
Dies at his home in Wilmslow; the inquest verdict, suicide, is later disputed.
The Prime Minister apologises on behalf of the government.

claims.statement: Alan Mathison Turing was born on 23 June 1912 in a nursing home in Paddington, London.

He was a long-distance runner: he built his strength in cross-country running, was known for running to scientific meetings, and in 1951 was still training for long-distance running on the roads around Wilmslow, where he had bought his first house.

After reporting a burglary at his home in 1952 he was arrested over a relationship with another man and tried on 31 March 1952 for "gross indecency"; rather than go to prison he accepted, for a year, oestrogen treatment intended to neutralise his libido.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Same-sex relations between men were then a crime in England; the treatment was imposed as the alternative to a prison sentence, not chosen as care.

claims.statement: His biographer Andrew Hodges writes that the drug was probably stilboestrol, a synthetic oestrogen; the 2009 government statement and other sources describe the treatment as a series of injections of female hormones.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The exact preparation and route are not settled in the sources read.

claims.statement: Hodges describes the injurious and humiliating effect of the hormones on his body; it is often repeated that the treatment made him grow breasts, though he is known to have mentioned this only once.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Breast growth (gynecomastia) is an expected effect of high-dose oestrogen in a man.

claims.statement: In a letter of 23 November 1952 he wrote that he had decided to have "another, and rather more co-operative go at a psychiatrist"; this was Jungian analysis with a refugee analyst, and he became very enthusiastic about it and wrote down all his dreams.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Seeking analysis is documented; no psychiatric diagnosis is recorded in the sources read.

claims.statement: His conviction led to the removal of his security clearance, so that he could no longer work for Government Communications Headquarters as he had since the war.
After the trial he returned to a wide range of academic work, including morphogenesis, quantum theory, and relativity, at Manchester University.
He died on 7 June 1954 at his home in Wilmslow, Cheshire, of cyanide poisoning, and the coroner's verdict was suicide.

In 2012 Professor Jack Copeland argued that the inquest evidence would not today support a suicide verdict, that friends had described him as cheerful in the days before he died, and that accidental inhalation of cyanide from a home electrolysis experiment was equally likely.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A retrospective challenge to the inquest finding; the cause of death remains disputed.

claims.statement: Hodges judges it more credible that Turing ended his own life and arranged matters so that it could be taken for an accident.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A biographer's interpretation; it conflicts with CLM-0010.

claims.statement: On 10 September 2009 the Prime Minister apologised on behalf of the British government, calling his treatment inhumane and describing his sentence as chemical castration by a series of injections of female hormones, accepted as the alternative to prison.

On 24 December 2013 he received a posthumous royal pardon; the Justice Secretary called the conviction unjust and discriminatory, and the Prime Minister said the sentence of chemical castration had caused physical and emotional damage.

The roster lists depression as a primary condition; the sources read document his prosecution, the hormone treatment, and his decision to seek Jungian analysis, but record no diagnosis of depression, so a depressive illness is a retrospective interpretation.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective and uncertain; it must not be read as a documented diagnosis.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Recognize and manage the harm of high-dose estrogen given to a 40-year-old gay man without his free and informed consent: evaluate gynecomastia as the EAA 2019 guideline advises (history, breast and testicular examination, testosterone, estradiol, LH, FSH, prolactin, SHBG, hCG, AFP, liver, kidney, and thyroid tests, scrotal ultrasound, breast imaging only if the examination is equivocal), name the cause as iatrogenic, stop the exposure, monitor recovery of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis without testosterone therapy while it recovers, protect bone health, and offer surgery if gynecomastia persists; treat a moderate depressive episode with measurement-based care, gay-affirming psychotherapy, and an antidepressant only if he chooses one, with a structured suicide-risk assessment, a safety plan, and the 988 Lifeline; offer HIV and STI testing and a PrEP discussion as routine adult care with his consent; and practise LGBTQ-affirming primary care. Sexual orientation is recorded as part of his social history, never as a problem, and every test and treatment requires his free, informed consent.

documentation.chief_complaint: Two-week follow-up; endocrinology consultation and scrotal ultrasound today

hpi.narrative: Mr. Turing returns two weeks after his first visit, five weeks after the last estrogen injection. He saw Dr. Montrose-Adeyemi of endocrinology this morning and had a scrotal ultrasound, which was normal. His breasts are still tender against his shirt, with no change in size, and he has had no nipple discharge. Libido and morning erections are still absent. He has had two sessions with the clinic psychologist and found them easier than he expected; they have begun with what was done to him rather than with his sexuality, which he says he has never regarded as the problem. He sleeps five to six hours and has run twice this week, alone. He has had no suicidal thoughts and keeps his safety plan on his phone. He takes cholecalciferol daily.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Turing returns eight weeks after his first visit, about eleven weeks after the last estrogen injection. The breast tenderness is less and he no longer notices it when running. Morning erections returned three weeks ago and his libido is coming back. He has had seven psychotherapy sessions and runs about 25 km a week. His mood is somewhat better, but he still feels flat most days, has little pleasure outside work, and wakes early. He has had no suicidal thoughts. After the last visit he asked to think about medicine; today, after a discussion of sertraline, mirtazapine, and bupropion and their effects on sexual function, weight, sleep, and blood pressure, he chose bupropion. He has no history of seizures, head injury, or an eating disorder and drinks little alcohol.

How quickly should the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis recover, and how should we monitor it?
Is testosterone therapy, tamoxifen, or an aromatase inhibitor indicated now?
How should we protect and assess his bone health?
When should surgery be considered if the gynecomastia persists?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Turing is seen at the request of Dr. Hallam, five weeks after the last of about a year of high-dose estrogen injections that were imposed on him abroad as the alternative to imprisonment. He did not consent freely and will not take them again. Breast enlargement began within a few months of the injections and became tender; libido and erections were lost over the same months. He has no testicular pain or swelling, nipple discharge, headache, visual disturbance, or galactorrhea. He has never used anabolic steroids, androgens, or other drugs linked to gynecomastia and has no liver, kidney, or thyroid disease. He has had no leg swelling, chest pain, or breathlessness. He runs 20 to 40 km a week. His sexual orientation was discussed only as he chose; it has no bearing on these findings. He asked for each step of the examination to be explained, and agreed to each
consultant_note.data_reviewed: The intake results, today's estradiol of 46 pg/mL and LH of 0.9 mIU/mL, and today's scrotal ultrasound, which shows testes of about 15 mL each, homogeneous, with no mass and no varicocele

exam.finding: Tall, lean man; normal male hair distribution
Examined with his agreement: firm, tender, rubbery, symmetric glandular tissue about 4 cm across behind each nipple; no discrete or eccentric mass, skin change, nipple discharge, or axillary nodes
Examined with his agreement: testes soft and slightly small without masses, as the ultrasound confirms
No thyroid enlargement

assessment.assessment: True gynecomastia, typical on examination and fully explained by a year of high-dose exogenous estrogen. hCG and AFP are normal and the scrotal ultrasound shows no mass, so a testicular tumor is excluded; liver, kidney, and thyroid disease are excluded. Breast imaging is not needed because the examination is typical and shows no discrete mass. Most gynecomastia of recent onset regresses once the cause is removed, though tissue present for many months may become fibrous and persist

Suppression of LH, FSH, and testosterone by exogenous estrogen, with estradiol already falling. Recovery is expected over two to six months. Testosterone therapy would suppress the axis again and is not indicated for a transient, drug-induced deficiency. Tamoxifen and aromatase inhibitors are not justified in general and are not needed here. The mildly raised prolactin is an expected estrogen effect and should be rechecked after the estrogen clears; no pituitary imaging is needed unless it stays raised

assessment.display: Adverse effects of high-dose estrogen given without free consent
assessment.assessment: An iatrogenic harm. He has no symptoms or signs of venous thrombosis, and his liver tests are normal. The treatment had no medical indication
Appropriate to replace while testosterone is low

recommendations: No further estrogen; watchful waiting for the gynecomastia
No testosterone therapy, tamoxifen, or aromatase inhibitor while the axis recovers
Testosterone, estradiol, LH, FSH, prolactin, and hemoglobin about six weeks from now, then every six to eight weeks until normal; testosterone and estradiol once more at about six months
Continue cholecalciferol 1,000 units daily, calcium from food, and running with strength work; a bone density scan only if hypogonadism persists beyond six months or a fragility fracture occurs
Breast imaging only if the examination becomes equivocal or a discrete mass appears
A plastic surgery opinion if the gynecomastia persists about twelve months after the estrogen stopped and he wants it removed
Return to endocrinology if testosterone remains low or LH and FSH have not recovered six months after the last dose, or if prolactin stays raised
